claim: Toxoplasma gondii chronically infects approximately 30% of the world's population.
source: Toxoplasma, specifically, is one of the most prevalent human pathogens, chronically infecting ~30% of the world's population (Swapna and Parkinson, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Swapna and Parkinson, 2017.

claim: In congenitally infected and immunocompromised patients, Toxoplasma disease outcomes are often severe and potentially fatal.
source: While most infections are asymptomatic, in congenitally infected and immunocompromised patients, disease outcomes are often severe and potentially fatal (Halonen and Weiss, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Halonen and Weiss, 2013.

claim: Toxoplasma gondii utilizes gliding motility that relies on actin and an unconventional myosin motor.
source: To facilitate these processes, Toxoplasma utilises a unique form of locomotion, called gliding motility, which relies on actin and an unconventional myosin motor (Frénal et al., 2017a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Frénal et al., 2017a.

claim: Toxoplasma gondii undergoes a unique form of cell division called endodyogeny where two daughter cells are synchronously assembled within the mother cell.
source: Within the parasitophorous vacuole, Toxoplasma begins a unique form of cell division called endodyogeny (Sheffield and Melton, 1968). Here, two daughter cells are synchronously assembled within the mother cell before daughter cell budding (Delbac et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sheffield and Melton, 1968 and Delbac et al., 2001.

claim: The apicoplast is a unique and essential organelle which contributes to isoprenoid synthesis.
source: During cell division, organelles such as mitochondria and the apicoplast, a unique and essential organelle which contributes to isoprenoid synthesis (Vaishnava and Striepen, 2006), also divide and are distributed between the two daughter parasites.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vaishnava and Striepen, 2006.

claim: Formation of the characteristic rosette pattern requires actin, several myosins, and other actin-binding proteins.
source: Formation of the characteristic rosette pattern requires actin, several myosins, and other actin-binding proteins (Frénal et al., 2017b; Haase et al., 2015; Jacot et al., 2013; Periz et al., 2017; Tosetti et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: As much as 98% of parasite actin is monomeric (G-actin) and not incorporated into filaments (F-actin).
source: Despite this crucial role in apicomplexan biology, there has been difficulty visualising actin filaments in apicomplexan species (Bannister and Mitchell, 1995; Sahoo et al., 2006; Shaw and Tilney, 1999) and it has been suggested that as much as 98% of parasite actin is monomeric (G-actin) and not incorporated into filaments (F-actin) (Dobrowolski et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dobrowolski et al., 1997.

claim: Toxoplasma F-actin has reduced stability, forming abnormally short filaments that are rapidly recycled.
source: This, along with structural differences found in actin of Apicomplexa (Pospich et al., 2017), led to the hypothesis that Toxoplasma F-actin has reduced stability, forming abnormally short filaments that are rapidly recycled to maintain essential cellular function (Pospich et al., 2017; Skillman et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pospich et al., 2017 and Skillman et al., 2011.

claim: The actin-chromobody has allowed for the visualisation of F-actin structures both in the parasite and extensive networks within the parasitophorous vacuole.
source: However, recent development of the actin-chromobody has allowed for the visualisation of F-actin structures both in the parasite and extensive networks within the parasitophorous vacuole (Periz et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Periz et al., 2017.

claim: Toxoplasma possesses a reduced repertoire of actin binding proteins, including ADF, profilin, coronin and cyclase-associated protein (CAP).
source: Actin turnover is regulated by actin binding proteins, of which Toxoplasma possesses a reduced repertoire, including ADF, profilin, coronin and cyclase-associated protein (CAP) (Baum et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Baum et al., 2006.

claim: ADF and profilin are essential for Toxoplasma progression through the lytic cycle.
source: Functional studies have shown ADF and profilin to be essential for Toxoplasma progression through the lytic cycle, while coronin depletion had a modest impact on parasite invasion and egress (Mehta and Sibley, 2011; Plattner et al., 2008; Salamun et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mehta and Sibley, 2011; Plattner et al., 2008; Salamun et al., 2014.

claim: Coronin depletion had a modest impact on parasite invasion and egress.
source: Functional studies have shown ADF and profilin to be essential for Toxoplasma progression through the lytic cycle, while coronin depletion had a modest impact on parasite invasion and egress (Mehta and Sibley, 2011; Plattner et al., 2008; Salamun et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mehta and Sibley, 2011; Plattner et al., 2008; Salamun et al., 2014.

claim: Species belonging to the Apicomplexa phylum possess a truncated form of CAP, retaining only the conserved C-terminal G-actin-binding CARP domain.
source: However, species belonging to the Apicomplexa phylum possess a truncated form of CAP, retaining only the conserved C-terminal G-actin-binding CARP domain (Hliscs et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hliscs et al., 2010.

claim: Biochemical analysis of Cryptosporidium parvum CAP identified the formation of a dimer and G-actin sequestering activity.
source: Biochemical analysis of Cryptosporidium parvum CAP identified the formation of a dimer and G-actin sequestering activity, while Plasmodium falciparum CAP was shown to facilitate nucleotide exchange, loading ADP-actin monomers with ATP (Hliscs et al., 2010; Makkonen et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hliscs et al., 2010 and Makkonen et al., 2013.

claim: Plasmodium falciparum CAP was shown to facilitate nucleotide exchange, loading ADP-actin monomers with ATP.
source: Biochemical analysis of Cryptosporidium parvum CAP identified the formation of a dimer and G-actin sequestering activity, while Plasmodium falciparum CAP was shown to facilitate nucleotide exchange, loading ADP-actin monomers with ATP (Hliscs et al., 2010; Makkonen et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hliscs et al., 2010 and Makkonen et al., 2013.

claim: A Plasmodium berghei CAP KO demonstrated that while PbCAP is dispensable for asexual blood stages in vivo, there is a complete defect in oocyst development in the insect vector.
source: A Plasmodium berghei CAP KO demonstrated that while PbCAP is dispensable for asexual blood stages in vivo, there is a complete defect in oocyst development in the insect vector which was overcome through complementation with C. parvum CAP (Hliscs et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hliscs et al., 2010.

claim: CAP localises to the apex of intracellular parasites.
source: While CAP has yet to be functionally characterised in Toxoplasma, Lorestani et al reported that CAP localises to the apex of intracellular parasites, a hub for events leading to egress and motility (Graindorge et al., 2016; Lorestani et al., 2012; Tosetti et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Graindorge et al., 2016; Lorestani et al., 2012; Tosetti et al., 2019.

claim: Following host cell lysis, relocalisation of CAP to the parasite cytosol was observed.
source: Intriguingly, following host cell lysis, relocalisation of CAP to the parasite cytosol was observed (Lorestani et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lorestani et al., 2012.

claim: Differential phosphorylation of CAP was identified in parasites with a delayed egress phenotype.
source: Furthermore, we have previously identified differential phosphorylation of CAP in parasites with a delayed egress phenotype (Treeck et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Treeck et al., 2014.

claim: T. gondii CAP is produced in two distinctly localised isoforms through alternative translation initiation: a membrane bound isoform, localised to the apical tip (longCAP) and a cytosolically dispersed isoform (shortCAP).
source: Here we show that T. gondii CAP is produced in two distinctly localised isoforms through alternative translation initiation: a membrane bound isoform, localised to the apical tip (longCAP) and a cytosolically dispersed isoform (shortCAP).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript showing differential localization of CAP isoforms.

claim: Conditional knockout of CAP identified an important function of CAP in some, but not all, actin-dependent processes.
source: Conditional knockout of CAP, using a second generation DiCre strain, identified an important function of CAP in some, but not all, actin-dependent processes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from conditional knockout studies.

claim: Invasion, egress, motility, correct daughter cell orientation and dense granule trafficking were all perturbed in CAP depleted parasites.
source: Invasion, egress, motility, correct daughter cell orientation and dense granule trafficking were all perturbed in CAP depleted parasites, while apicoplast inheritance was not.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from phenotypic characterization of CAP depleted parasites.

claim: Apicoplast inheritance was not affected in CAP depleted parasites.
source: Invasion, egress, motility, correct daughter cell orientation and dense granule trafficking were all perturbed in CAP depleted parasites, while apicoplast inheritance was not.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing no defect in apicoplast segregation.

claim: The characteristic rosette organisation of parasites in the vacuole was completely lost in CAP depleted parasites.
source: Furthermore, the characteristic rosette organisation of parasites in the vacuole was completely lost, but synchronicity of division was largely unaffected.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing loss of rosetting in CAP depleted parasites.

claim: Synchronicity of division was largely unaffected in CAP depleted parasites.
source: Furthermore, the characteristic rosette organisation of parasites in the vacuole was completely lost, but synchronicity of division was largely unaffected.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing synchronous division in CAP depleted parasites.

claim: Rapid protein transfer only occurs between two adjacent cells in a vacuole in CAP depleted parasites.
source: Strikingly, while we observe rapid protein transfer only between two adjacent cells in a vacuole, all parasites remain connected through a decentralised residual body, potentially explaining why synchrony of division is unaffected.
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP experimental data.

claim: All parasites remain connected through a decentralised residual body in CAP depleted parasites.
source: Strikingly, while we observe rapid protein transfer only between two adjacent cells in a vacuole, all parasites remain connected through a decentralised residual body, potentially explaining why synchrony of division is unaffected.
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D electron microscopy data.

claim: CAP deletion leads to a dysregulation of actin in some, but not all subcellular localisations.
source: Using chromobody expressing parasites lines we show that CAP deletion leads to a dysregulation of actin in some, but not all subcellular localisations.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from chromobody expressing parasite lines.

claim: CAP-depleted type I RH parasites display normal lethality in the mouse in vivo infection model.
source: In the mouse in vivo infection model, CAP-depleted type I RH parasites display normal lethality, while CAP depletion renders type II Pru parasites avirulent, with markedly reduced cyst formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by mouse infection data.

claim: CAP depletion renders type II Pru parasites avirulent, with markedly reduced cyst formation.
source: In the mouse in vivo infection model, CAP-depleted type I RH parasites display normal lethality, while CAP depletion renders type II Pru parasites avirulent, with markedly reduced cyst formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by mouse infection data.

claim: The cytoplasmic isoform of CAP was sufficient for the infection of mice and the formation of latent stages in the brain.
source: Furthermore, the cytoplasmic isoform of CAP was sufficient for the infection of mice and the formation of latent stages in the brain, indicating that the apically localised CAP isoform provides only a small fitness benefit under the conditions tested here.
evidence: The claim is supported by mouse infection data with CAP isoform complemented parasites.

claim: T. gondii CAP contains a unique predicted N-terminal extension that is not present in other Apicomplexa, such as Plasmodium.
source: T. gondii CAP, and CAP from Neospora and Hammondia species contain a unique predicted N-terminal extension that is not present in other Apicomplexa, such as Plasmodium (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The N-terminal extension of T. gondii CAP contains two predicted palmitoylation sites.
source: The extension contains two predicted palmitoylation sites and CAP was identified in an analysis of palmitoylated proteins in Toxoplasma gondii (Foe et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Foe et al., 2015.

claim: CAP was identified in an analysis of palmitoylated proteins in Toxoplasma gondii.
source: The extension contains two predicted palmitoylation sites and CAP was identified in an analysis of palmitoylated proteins in Toxoplasma gondii (Foe et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Foe et al., 2015.

claim: Two phosphorylation sites in the N-terminus of T. gondii CAP are substantially phosphorylated upon ionophore-induced egress.
source: Furthermore, two phosphorylation sites in the N-terminus of T. gondii CAP are substantially phosphorylated upon ionophore-induced egress (Treeck et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Treeck et al., 2014.

claim: These phosphorylation events are dependent on the calcium-dependent kinase 3 (CDPK3).
source: These phosphorylation events are dependent on the calcium-dependent kinase 3 (CDPK3) (Treeck et al., 2014), which has been shown to be important in mediating rapid exit from the host cell and is localised to the plasma membrane (Black et al., 2000; Garrison et al., 2012; Lourido et al., 2012; McCoy et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Treeck et al., 2014 and other studies.

claim: CDPK3 has been shown to be important in mediating rapid exit from the host cell and is localised to the plasma membrane.
source: These phosphorylation events are dependent on the calcium-dependent kinase 3 (CDPK3) (Treeck et al., 2014), which has been shown to be important in mediating rapid exit from the host cell and is localised to the plasma membrane (Black et al., 2000; Garrison et al., 2012; Lourido et al., 2012; McCoy et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Black et al., 2000; Garrison et al., 2012; Lourido et al., 2012; McCoy et al., 2012.

claim: CAP-GFP localises to the apex of the parasite and to the cytoplasm of intracellular tachyzoites.
source: To visualise CAP we expressed it as a GFP fusion. CAP-GFP localises to the apex of the parasite, as previously shown, but also to the cytoplasm of intracellular tachyzoites (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Western blot analysis of parasite lysates revealed the presence of two bands close to the expected size of CAP.
source: Western blot analysis of parasite lysates revealed the presence of two bands close to the expected size of CAP, which are expressed at a constant level, relative to the Toxoplasma loading control, across the first 24 hr following host cell invasion (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The two CAP bands are expressed at a constant level, relative to the Toxoplasma loading control, across the first 24 hr following host cell invasion.
source: Western blot analysis of parasite lysates revealed the presence of two bands close to the expected size of CAP, which are expressed at a constant level, relative to the Toxoplasma loading control, across the first 24 hr following host cell invasion (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Sequence comparison of T. gondii CAP to P. falciparum CAP reveals a second in-frame methionine at position 37 in Toxoplasma that aligns with the P. falciparum CAP start methionine.
source: Indeed, sequence comparison of T. gondii CAP to P. falciparum CAP reveals a second in-frame methionine at position 37 in Toxoplasma that aligns with the P. falciparum CAP start methionine (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The M1 translation initiation sequence conforms less with the Toxoplasma Kozak sequence than the sequence preceding M37.
source: We therefore analysed the translation initiation sequence around CAP's first (M1) and second (M37) putative translational start sites. The M1 translation initiation sequence conforms less with the Toxoplasma Kozak sequence than the sequence preceding M37; as the former is lacking an adenine at the −3 position (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Mutants expressing shortCAP showed exclusively cytoplasmic staining while those expressing longCAP showed predominantly apical staining.
source: While WT CAP parasites showed the expected dual localisation, mutants expressing shortCAP showed exclusively cytoplasmic staining while those expressing longCAP showed predominantly apical staining, with some further signal throughout the parasite (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: CAP_C6,8A appeared cytosolic with no detectable accumulation of CAP at the apical end of the parasites.
source: We mutated the two cysteines in the N-terminus to alanine residues (CAP_C6,8A). CAP_C6,8A appeared cytosolic with no detectable accumulation of CAP at the apical end of the parasites (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Western blot analysis of the HA-tagged CAP variants confirmed that WT CAP is identified as two distinct protein bands, which correlate with the predicted size for longCAP and shortCAP.
source: Western blot analysis of the HA-tagged CAP variants confirmed that WT CAP is identified as two distinct protein bands, which correlate with the predicted size for longCAP and shortCAP (23.9 and 20 kDa).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data.

claim: Parasites expressing shortCAP displayed only the lower molecular weight band, while longCAP-expressing parasites only showed the higher molecular weight band.
source: Parasites expressing shortCAP displayed only the lower molecular weight band, while longCAP-expressing parasites only showed the higher molecular weight band.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data.

claim: The protein levels of longCAP appear reduced compared to its isoform in parasites expressing WT CAP, whereas the shortCAP isoform shows an increase.
source: We observed that the protein levels of longCAP appear reduced compared to its isoform in parasites expressing WT CAP, whereas the shortCAP isoform shows an increase (Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: In Toxoplasma, and potentially closely related coccidian parasites of Hammondia and Neospora, CAP is produced as two differentially localised isoforms using alternative translational start sites.
source: Collectively, these results show that in Toxoplasma, and potentially closely related coccidian parasites of Hammondia and Neospora, CAP is produced as two differentially localised isoforms using alternative translational start sites and the apical localisation of the long isoform is likely palmitoylation dependent.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on CAP isoforms and sequence analysis.

claim: The apical localisation of the long isoform is likely palmitoylation dependent.
source: Collectively, these results show that in Toxoplasma, and potentially closely related coccidian parasites of Hammondia and Neospora, CAP is produced as two differentially localised isoforms using alternative translational start sites and the apical localisation of the long isoform is likely palmitoylation dependent.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that mutation of putative palmitoylation sites abolishes apical localization.

claim: The new DiCre_T2A line excision efficiency varied between 98% and 99% for replicates on day 1 and was maintained throughout the experiment with a maximal loss of 3% of excision efficiency by day 65.
source: The new DiCre_T2A line excision efficiency varied between 98% and 99% for replicates on day 1 and was maintained throughout the experiment with a maximal loss of 3% of excision efficiency, irrespective of the presence or absence of chloramphenicol selection, by day 65 (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The original DiCre line, cultured under standard non-stress conditions, lost 42% of excision capacity by day 65.
source: In contrast, the original DiCre line, cultured under standard non-stress conditions, lost 42% of excision capacity by day 65 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), although this was only done as a single replicate.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The second generation DiCre line, RH DiCre_T2A ∆ku80∆hxgprt, retains high excision capacity over long periods of time, even when exposed to extracellular stress.
source: This shows that the second generation DiCre line, RH DiCre_T2A ∆ku80∆hxgprt, retains high excision capacity over long periods of time, even when exposed to extracellular stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing the new and original DiCre lines.

claim: RAP treatment resulted in a complete loss of CAP in the LoxPCAP line.
source: RAP treatment resulted in a complete loss of CAP (∆CAP), as shown by IFA (Figure 3C) and Western blot (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by IFA and Western blot data shown in Figures 3C and 3E.

claim: After 15 days in growth competition with ∆CAPCAP, ∆CAP parasites were largely depleted (>97.3%) from the population.
source: After 15 days in growth competition with ∆CAPCAP, ∆CAP parasites were largely depleted (>97.3%) from the population, while ∆CAPshortCAP showed a reduction of only 4%.
evidence: The claim is supported by competition assay data.

claim: ∆CAPshortCAP showed a reduction of only 4% after 15 days in growth competition with ∆CAPCAP.
source: After 15 days in growth competition with ∆CAPCAP, ∆CAP parasites were largely depleted (>97.3%) from the population, while ∆CAPshortCAP showed a reduction of only 4%.
evidence: The claim is supported by competition assay data.

claim: ∆CAPlongCAP showed an intermediate level of depletion (33.3%) after 15 days in growth competition with ∆CAPCAP.
source: In contrast, ∆CAPlongCAP showed an intermediate level of depletion (33.3%).
evidence: The claim is supported by competition assay data.

claim: After 30 days in culture, ∆CAP parasites were largely depleted (>99.9%).
source: These phenotypes were exaggerated after 30 days in culture; ∆CAP parasites were largely depleted (>99.9%), ∆CAPshortCAP showed a reduction of 12.4%, and ∆CAPlongCAP growth was reduced by 43.1% relative to ∆CAPCAP (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by competition assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ∆CAPshortCAP showed a reduction of 12.4% after 30 days in culture.
source: These phenotypes were exaggerated after 30 days in culture; ∆CAP parasites were largely depleted (>99.9%), ∆CAPshortCAP showed a reduction of 12.4%, and ∆CAPlongCAP growth was reduced by 43.1% relative to ∆CAPCAP (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by competition assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ∆CAPlongCAP growth was reduced by 43.1% relative to ∆CAPCAP after 30 days in culture.
source: These phenotypes were exaggerated after 30 days in culture; ∆CAP parasites were largely depleted (>99.9%), ∆CAPshortCAP showed a reduction of 12.4%, and ∆CAPlongCAP growth was reduced by 43.1% relative to ∆CAPCAP (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by competition assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: CAP plays an important but non-essential role in cell culture.
source: Collectively, these findings demonstrate that CAP plays an important but non-essential role in cell culture and that its function can be largely restored by the short CAP isoform but only partially by the long isoform.
evidence: The claim is supported by competition assay data.

claim: CAP function can be largely restored by the short CAP isoform but only partially by the long isoform.
source: Collectively, these findings demonstrate that CAP plays an important but non-essential role in cell culture and that its function can be largely restored by the short CAP isoform but only partially by the long isoform.
evidence: The claim is supported by competition assay data.

claim: In the absence of CAP (ΔCAP), significantly fewer parasites are able to initiate gliding motility in 3D motility assays compared to the RH strain.
source: In the absence of CAP (ΔCAP), significantly fewer parasites are able to initiate gliding motility in 3D motility assays (Leung et al., 2014) compared to the RH strain (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D motility assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In the motile population of ∆CAP parasites, trajectory displacement, trajectory length and maximum achieved speeds were all reduced.
source: In the motile population, trajectory displacement, trajectory length and maximum achieved speeds were all reduced, while mean speed was not significantly different (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D motility assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Mean speed was not significantly different in the motile population of ∆CAP parasites.
source: In the motile population, trajectory displacement, trajectory length and maximum achieved speeds were all reduced, while mean speed was not significantly different (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D motility assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Both ∆CAPshortCAP and ∆CAPlongCAP parasites showed no significant differences in motility initiation, track displacement, track length and speed compared to ∆CAPCAP.
source: Both ∆CAPshortCAP and ∆CAPlongCAP parasites showed no significant differences in motility initiation, track displacement, track length and speed compared to ∆CAPCAP. (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D motility assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: ∆CAP showed a reduction of invasion capacity (50.2% reduction compared to the WT complemented line).
source: ∆CAP showed a reduction of invasion capacity (50.2% reduction compared to the WT complemented line), which was restored by both the short and long isoforms (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by invasion assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The invasion defect in ∆CAP was restored by both the short and long isoforms.
source: ∆CAP showed a reduction of invasion capacity (50.2% reduction compared to the WT complemented line), which was restored by both the short and long isoforms (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by invasion assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: ∆CAP parasites showed a substantial delay in egress from host cells at 30 s after induction (73.1% less egress in ∆CAP compared to ∆CAPCAP).
source: ∆CAP parasites showed a substantial delay in egress from host cells at 30 s after induction (73.1% less egress in ∆CAP compared to ∆CAPCAP), while at 2 min the majority of parasites have egressed (10.6% less egress in ∆CAP compared to ∆CAPCAP) (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by egress assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: At 2 min after induction, the majority of ∆CAP parasites have egressed (10.6% less egress in ∆CAP compared to ∆CAPCAP).
source: ∆CAP parasites showed a substantial delay in egress from host cells at 30 s after induction (73.1% less egress in ∆CAP compared to ∆CAPCAP), while at 2 min the majority of parasites have egressed (10.6% less egress in ∆CAP compared to ∆CAPCAP) (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by egress assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The egress defect in ∆CAP was fully restored in ∆CAPshortCAP parasites.
source: This defect was fully restored in ∆CAPshortCAP parasites, while ∆CAPlongCAP showed slightly lower levels of egress after 30 s of treatment but by 60 s were indistinguishable from WT or short CAP complemented lines.
evidence: The claim is supported by egress assay data.

claim: ∆CAPlongCAP showed slightly lower levels of egress after 30 s of treatment but by 60 s were indistinguishable from WT or short CAP complemented lines.
source: This defect was fully restored in ∆CAPshortCAP parasites, while ∆CAPlongCAP showed slightly lower levels of egress after 30 s of treatment but by 60 s were indistinguishable from WT or short CAP complemented lines.
evidence: The claim is supported by egress assay data.

claim: Both the mean run length and the mean velocity of dense granules were significantly increased in ∆CAP (34.8% and 52.9%, respectively).
source: Both the mean run length and the mean velocity were significantly increased in ∆CAP (34.8% and 52.9%, respectively), but not in either of the complements.
evidence: The claim is supported by dense granule trafficking assay data.

claim: The mean run length and mean velocity of dense granules were not significantly increased in either of the CAP complements.
source: Both the mean run length and the mean velocity were significantly increased in ∆CAP (34.8% and 52.9%, respectively), but not in either of the complements.
evidence: The claim is supported by dense granule trafficking assay data.

claim: Both CAP isoforms play a supporting role in dense granule trafficking.
source: These results indicate that both CAP isoforms play a supporting role in dense granule trafficking and that, upon CAP deletion, dense granules are trafficked further distances at higher speed.
evidence: The claim is supported by dense granule trafficking assay data.

claim: Upon CAP deletion, dense granules are trafficked further distances at higher speed.
source: These results indicate that both CAP isoforms play a supporting role in dense granule trafficking and that, upon CAP deletion, dense granules are trafficked further distances at higher speed.
evidence: The claim is supported by dense granule trafficking assay data.

claim: CAP plays a role in the actin-dependent processes of motility, invasion, egress, and dense granule trafficking.
source: Collectively these data show that CAP plays a role in the actin-dependent processes described above and that either isoform is able to fulfil these CAP functions.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple phenotypic assays.

claim: Either CAP isoform is able to fulfil CAP functions in motility, invasion, egress, and dense granule trafficking.
source: Collectively these data show that CAP plays a role in the actin-dependent processes described above and that either isoform is able to fulfil these CAP functions.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple phenotypic assays.

claim: Upon CAP deletion, a complete loss of the characteristic rosette formation normally seen in Toxoplasma was observed.
source: Upon CAP deletion, we observed a complete loss of the characteristic rosette formation normally seen in Toxoplasma.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data.

claim: The aberrant rosetting phenotype was fully rescued upon complementation with either WT CAP or the short CAP isoform.
source: This aberrant phenotype was fully rescued upon complementation with either WT CAP or the short CAP isoform (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ∆CAPlongCAP displayed partial restoration with 44.9% of parasites forming phenotypically normal rosettes while the remainder were disorganised within the vacuole.
source: ∆CAPlongCAP displayed partial restoration with 44.9% of parasites forming phenotypically normal rosettes while the remainder were disorganised within the vacuole.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data.

claim: The WT-complemented ∆CAPCAP photobleached parasites display rapid recovery of fluorescence to which, in most cases, all parasites in the vacuole appear to contribute.
source: As expected, the WT-complemented ∆CAPCAP photobleached parasites display rapid recovery of fluorescence to which, in most cases, all parasites in the vacuole appear to contribute (Figure 5Bi and C and Video 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5Bi and C.

claim: ∆CAP photobleached parasites were supported in their rapid fluorescence recovery predominantly by just one other parasite, usually the parasite closest to the bleached cell, resulting in slow recovery.
source: Conversely, ∆CAP photobleached parasites were supported in their rapid fluorescence recovery predominantly by just one other parasite, usually the parasite closest to the bleached cell, resulting in slow recovery (Figure 5Bii and C and Video 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5Bii and C.

claim: RTORP between parasites was not negatively affected in RH ∆ku80∆gra2 parasites where the IVN fails to form.
source: To determine whether the observed defect in the RTORP was dependent on the presence of the IVN, we performed a FRAP assay in RH ∆ku80∆gra2 parasites (Rommereim et al., 2016) where the IVN fails to form but parasites still organise in rosettes. The results show that RTORP between parasites was not negatively affected (Figure 5Biii and Video 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5Biii.

claim: The IVN is unlikely involved in cell-cell communication.
source: The IVN, therefore, is unlikely involved in cell-cell communication.
evidence: The claim is inferred from FRAP data showing normal RTORP in ∆gra2 parasites lacking the IVN.

claim: If ∆CAPlongCAP parasites rosette, they show normal RTORP between all cells in the vacuole.
source: These experiments revealed that if ∆CAPlongCAP parasites rosette, they show normal RTORP between all cells in the vacuole, while non-rosetting parasites display the same defect as the ∆CAP line, with fluorescence recovery from only one other parasite in the vacuole (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Non-rosetting ∆CAPlongCAP parasites display the same defect as the ∆CAP line, with fluorescence recovery from only one other parasite in the vacuole.
source: These experiments revealed that if ∆CAPlongCAP parasites rosette, they show normal RTORP between all cells in the vacuole, while non-rosetting parasites display the same defect as the ∆CAP line, with fluorescence recovery from only one other parasite in the vacuole (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: ∆CAP and non-rosetting ∆CAPlongCAP photobleached parasites recovered significantly less fluorescence than their rosetting counterparts.
source: As expected, ∆CAP and non-rosetting ∆CAPlongCAP photobleached parasites recovered significantly less fluorescence than their rosetting counterparts (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Only parasite pairs in close proximity are rapidly communicating in ∆CAP vacuoles.
source: This revealed that only parasite pairs in close proximity are rapidly communicating.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequential photobleaching FRAP data.

claim: CAP deletion leads to a loss of both rosetting and the rapid transfer of reporter proteins between more than two parasites.
source: Collectively the results show that CAP deletion leads to a loss of both rosetting and the rapid transfer of reporter proteins between more than two parasites.
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP and microscopy data.

claim: RTORP appears to be dependent on parasite rosette organisation, but not on presence of the IVN.
source: Furthermore, RTORP appears to be dependent on parasite rosette organisation, but not on presence of the IVN.
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP data from rosetting and non-rosetting parasites and from ∆gra2 parasites.

claim: At 20 hr post-infection, in the complete absence of rosettes, ∆CAP vacuoles exhibited synchronous division with no significant difference to the WT complemented line (98.3% and 99.6% synchronous division, respectively).
source: At 20 hr post-infection, in the complete absence of rosettes, ∆CAP vacuoles exhibited synchronous division with no significant difference to the WT complemented line (98.3% and 99.6% synchronous division, respectively). (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by IMC3 staining data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: At 24 hr and 30 hr post-infection, synchronous division was reduced to 93.4% and 87.8%, respectively, in the ∆CAP line.
source: At 24 hr and 30 hr post-infection, synchronous division was reduced to 93.4% and 87.8%, respectively, in the ∆CAP line (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by IMC3 staining data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: While in WT CAP complemented parasites 94.6% of daughter cells grew in the same orientation, a significant defect was observed in ∆CAP and ∆CAPlongCAP strains; only 42.9% (∆CAP) and 67.7% (∆CAPlongCAP) of daughter cells orientated in the same direction.
source: While in WT CAP complemented parasites 94.6% of daughter cells grew in the same orientation, a significant defect was observed in ∆CAP and ∆CAPlongCAP strains; only 42.9% (∆CAP) and 67.7% (∆CAPlongCAP) of daughter cells orientated in the same direction.
evidence: The claim is supported by IMC3 staining data.

claim: ∆CAPshortCAP parasites were able to largely overcome the daughter cell orientation defect, with 89.5% of daughter cells growing in the same orientation.
source: ∆CAPshortCAP parasites were able to largely overcome this defect, with 89.5% of daughter cells growing in the same orientation (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by IMC3 staining data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: No significant differences in apicoplast inheritance rates were identified between ∆CAPCAP and ∆CAP strains.
source: Using streptavidin as a marker for the apicoplast, we identified no significant differences in apicoplast inheritance rates between ∆CAPCAP and ∆CAP strains (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by apicoplast segregation assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the ∆CAPCAP strain, all parasites in the vacuole contribute to recovery of a photobleached parasite.
source: In the ∆CAPCAP strain, as expected for a WT complemented line, all parasites in the vacuole contribute to recovery of a photobleached parasite (Figure 7A) and a normal centralised residual body is formed, connecting all parasites in the vacuole (Figure 7B and Video 8), with one tubular extension extending away from the residual body with no apparent connections at the distal end.
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP and FIB SEM data shown in Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: A normal centralised residual body is formed in ∆CAPCAP parasites, connecting all parasites in the vacuole.
source: In the ∆CAPCAP strain, as expected for a WT complemented line, all parasites in the vacuole contribute to recovery of a photobleached parasite (Figure 7A) and a normal centralised residual body is formed, connecting all parasites in the vacuole (Figure 7B and Video 8), with one tubular extension extending away from the residual body with no apparent connections at the distal end.
evidence: The claim is supported by FIB SEM data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: For the ∆CAP strain, fluorescence recovery of the photobleached parasite was predominantly observed from those cells in close proximity.
source: In contrast, for the ∆CAP strain, fluorescence recovery of the photobleached parasite was predominantly observed from those cells in close proximity (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: FIB SEM images revealed membrane bound tubular connections of approximately 300 nm thickness between ∆CAP parasites.
source: To investigate how these parasites are connected, we analysed FIB SEM images obtained from the photobleached vacuole in Figure 7C. This revealed membrane bound tubular connections of approximately 300 nm thickness between parasites, despite the aberrant transfer of mCherry and loss of rosetting (Figure 7Di and ii).
evidence: The claim is supported by FIB SEM data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: All parasites in the ∆CAP vacuole are connected by tubular connections, likely representing a decentralised residual body.
source: Following the lumen of the connections across three dimensions demonstrates that all parasites in the vacuole are connected by these tubular connections, likely representing a decentralised residual body that forms as a result of an inability to keep the posterior ends of the parasites in close proximity (Figure 7D.iii, Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Video 9).
evidence: The claim is supported by FIB SEM data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Rapid transfer of mCherry was always between parasites in close proximity at their basal ends in ∆CAP vacuoles.
source: Correlation of the FRAP data with the FIB SEM images showed that rapid transfer of mCherry was always between parasites in close proximity at their basal ends.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlative FRAP and FIB SEM data.

claim: Despite their disorganised appearance and loss of rapid cell-cell communication, ∆CAP parasites are still connected by a decentralised residual body.
source: The largely synchronous division in ∆CAP parasites could be explained by our CLEM results. Despite their disorganised appearance and loss of rapid cell-cell communication, ∆CAP parasites are still connected by a decentralised residual body.
evidence: The claim is supported by CLEM data.

claim: Rosetting and rapid cell-cell communication are not essential for synchronicity of division.
source: Whatever the basis for synchronicity is, rosetting and rapid cell-cell communication are not essential and their analysis cannot be reliably used to predict whether connections between parasites exist.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing synchronous division in ∆CAP parasites despite loss of rosetting and RTORP.

claim: Loss of CAP in Cb-EmFP ∆CAP parasites led to complete loss of parasite vacuole rosetting.
source: In agreement with our previous findings, deletion of CAP in the actin chromobody-labelled cells led to complete loss of parasite vacuole rosetting.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data of chromobody expressing parasites.

claim: After three rounds of division (eight parasites/vacuole) and onwards, loss of rosetting was accompanied by extensive filamentous structures of the chromobody throughout the parasitophorous vacuole in Cb-EmFP ∆CAP parasites.
source: After three rounds of division (eight parasites/vacuole) and onwards, loss of rosetting was accompanied by extensive filamentous structures of the chromobody throughout the parasitophorous vacuole (Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: A complete loss of the juxtanuclear actin polymerisation centre was observed in the Cb-EmFP ∆CAP line.
source: We observed a complete loss of the juxtanuclear actin polymerisation centre in the Cb-EmFP ∆CAP line, suggesting CAP plays a role in establishing this intracellular F-actin accumulation (Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: CAP plays a role in establishing the intracellular F-actin accumulation at the juxtanuclear region.
source: We observed a complete loss of the juxtanuclear actin polymerisation centre in the Cb-EmFP ∆CAP line, suggesting CAP plays a role in establishing this intracellular F-actin accumulation (Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the loss of the juxtanuclear actin polymerisation centre in CAP depleted parasites.

claim: WT CAP and shortCAP complementation restored the juxtanuclear actin polymerisation centre.
source: WT CAP and shortCAP complementation restored this actin polymerisation centre.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data of complemented chromobody expressing parasites.

claim: LongCAP complementation only rescued the juxtanuclear actin polymerisation centre in 11% of parasites, irrespective of rosetting.
source: LongCAP complementation only rescued it in 11% of parasites, irrespective of rosetting, which shows that the juxtanuclear actin accumulation and rosetting are not phenotypically linked (Figure 8E).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The juxtanuclear actin accumulation and rosetting are not phenotypically linked.
source: LongCAP complementation only rescued it in 11% of parasites, irrespective of rosetting, which shows that the juxtanuclear actin accumulation and rosetting are not phenotypically linked (Figure 8E).
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing that longCAP complementation rescues rosetting in some parasites but not the juxtanuclear actin centre.

claim: BIPPO treatment of both CAP knockout and WT CAP complemented lines led to a basal accumulation of F-actin.
source: BIPPO treatment of both CAP knockout and WT CAP complemented lines led to a basal accumulation of F-actin (Figure 8F), suggesting that CAP is not essential for this process.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: CAP is not essential for basal accumulation of F-actin following BIPPO stimulation.
source: BIPPO treatment of both CAP knockout and WT CAP complemented lines led to a basal accumulation of F-actin (Figure 8F), suggesting that CAP is not essential for this process.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing basal F-actin accumulation in both CAP knockout and complemented lines after BIPPO treatment.

claim: The accumulation of chromobody in the vacuole is found within regions of the tubular connections between parasites in Cb-EmFP ∆CAP parasites.
source: This analysis showed that the accumulation of chromobody in the vacuole is found within regions of the tubular connections between parasites.
evidence: The claim is supported by CLEM data.

claim: Tubular connections with strong chromobody accumulation appeared morphologically distinct from the other parts of the tubular connections with lower or undetectable chromobody signal in Cb-EmFP ∆CAP parasites.
source: Interestingly, tubular connections with strong chromobody accumulation appeared morphologically distinct from the other parts of the tubular connections with lower or undetectable chromobody signal.
evidence: The claim is supported by SBF SEM data.

claim: Tubules with low chromobody signal contain membranous structures within the tubule lumen in Cb-EmFP ∆CAP parasites.
source: Close examination of tubules with low chromobody signal revealed that they contain membranous structures within the tubule lumen (magenta 3D model and arrows) (Figure 9Biii and iv).
evidence: The claim is supported by SBF SEM data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Tubule regions with high chromobody signal were essentially devoid of any internal membranous structures in Cb-EmFP ∆CAP parasites.
source: In contrast, tubule regions with high chromobody signal were essentially devoid of any internal membranous structures (green 3D model and arrows) (Figure 9Bi and ii).
evidence: The claim is supported by SBF SEM data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The chromobody, and by extension F-actin, is found in most if not all tubular connections in Cb-EmFP ∆CAP parasites, although of varying intensity.
source: Collectively these results show that the chromobody, and by extension F-actin, is found in most if not all tubular connections, although of varying intensity.
evidence: The claim is supported by CLEM data.

claim: CAP deletion in the RH strain still results in high virulence in mice.
source: In both instances mice began to succumb to infection after 9 days, indicating that, despite the motility and rosetting phenotypes, CAP depletion in a type I RH background still results in high virulence in mice (Figure 10A).
evidence: The claim is supported by mouse survival data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: Upon injection of ~50,000 tachyzoites, Pru ∆CAP parasites showed no virulence in mice.
source: In stark contrast to the RH line, upon injection of ~50,000 tachyzoites, Pru ∆CAP parasites showed no virulence in mice while the Pru ∆CAPCAP, Pru ∆CAPshortCAP, and Pru ∆CAPlongCAP complemented parasites led to a lethal infection, with most mice succumbing to the parasites 8–10 days post-infection (Figure 10B).
evidence: The claim is supported by mouse survival data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: Pru ∆CAPCAP, Pru ∆CAPshortCAP, and Pru ∆CAPlongCAP complemented parasites led to a lethal infection, with most mice succumbing to the parasites 8–10 days post-infection.
source: In stark contrast to the RH line, upon injection of ~50,000 tachyzoites, Pru ∆CAP parasites showed no virulence in mice while the Pru ∆CAPCAP, Pru ∆CAPshortCAP, and Pru ∆CAPlongCAP complemented parasites led to a lethal infection, with most mice succumbing to the parasites 8–10 days post-infection (Figure 10B).
evidence: The claim is supported by mouse survival data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: Expression of either individual CAP isoform is sufficient to cause a lethal infection in mice.
source: These data show that expression of either individual isoform is sufficient to cause a lethal infection.
evidence: The claim is inferred from mouse survival data showing that both shortCAP and longCAP complemented parasites cause lethal infections.

claim: Both the Pru ∆CAP and Pru ∆CAPlongCAP infections demonstrated considerably lower cyst loads compared to Pru ∆CAPCAP and Pru ∆CAPshortCAP infected mice.
source: Both the Pru ∆CAP and Pru ∆CAPlongCAP infections demonstrated considerably lower cyst loads compared to Pru ∆CAPCAP and Pru ∆CAPshortCAP infected mice (Figure 10D).
evidence: The claim is supported by cyst burden data shown in Figure 10D.

claim: CAP plays an essential role in the virulence of the type II Pru parasite strain, but not the type I RH strain.
source: These results show that CAP plays an essential role in the virulence of the type II Pru parasite strain, but not the type I RH strain.
evidence: The claim is supported by mouse infection data showing differential virulence of CAP depleted RH and Pru strains.

claim: The short CAP isoform is able to fulfil all functions of CAP in cell culture and in the mouse model.
source: Moreover, while the short CAP isoform is able to fulfil all functions of CAP in cell culture and in the mouse model, the long isoform, despite its ability to complement most phenotypes to at least ~50% of WT complement levels, has a significant defect in establishing a chronic infection at the infectious dose used here.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple phenotypic assays and mouse infection data.

claim: The long isoform has a significant defect in establishing a chronic infection at the infectious dose used.
source: Moreover, while the short CAP isoform is able to fulfil all functions of CAP in cell culture and in the mouse model, the long isoform, despite its ability to complement most phenotypes to at least ~50% of WT complement levels, has a significant defect in establishing a chronic infection at the infectious dose used here.
evidence: The claim is supported by cyst burden data in mice.
